title: Manaslu Expedition: Full Guide
excerpt: Manaslu, 8,163 m, is a peak above 8,000 m in central Nepal. The full guide: the approach trek, rotations, technical sections, oxygen, Sherpa support, requirements and cost.
seoTitle: Manaslu Expedition: Route, Oxygen, Sherpas, Requirements and Cost

content.value: On day 24 of the expedition, before dawn, climbers leave the high camp by the light of their headlamps for the summit of Manaslu, 8,163 m (26,781 ft). A Manaslu expedition is a 30-day climbing expedition in Nepal to the eighth highest mountain in the world, a peak above 8,000 m that is considered one of the more technically accessible, but is far from easy. It is meant only for climbers who have already gained experience on peaks of 6,000 and 7,000 m. The expedition includes an approach trek of about a week, about two weeks of rotations and acclimatization between the high camps, glacier travel past crevasses, climbing along fixed ropes, bottled oxygen and a personal Sherpa guide for every climber, and it departs in September, in the fall season.

Anyone considering a peak above 8,000 m needs an accurate picture before deciding, not just summit photos. This guide is based on the expedition we run, and explains how you reach base camp, how the rotations work, where the technical sections are, what the oxygen and the Sherpas do, what is required of you before registering and what it costs.
What Manaslu is, and why this mountain

Manaslu, the "Mountain of the Spirit", rises to 8,163 m in Gorkha district in central Nepal, close to the border with Tibet, and it is one of the 14 mountains in the world whose summits stand above 8,000 m. Its base camp lies above the village of Sama Gaun, and from it climbs the normal route, on the northeast face of the mountain, which most expeditions follow.

Manaslu is considered one of the more technically accessible of the mountains above 8,000 m, which is why many see it as the gateway to the world of the highest mountains. But accessible is not easy. The climb crosses crevassed glaciers and steep snow and ice slopes, at an altitude where every step takes effort, the cold is extreme and the weather can close the mountain for days. The mountain demands excellent fitness, mental preparation and close professional support, so the expedition is built around a long itinerary, oxygen and a personal Sherpa guide for every climber.
The approach trek: over the Larke La into the Budhi Gandaki valley

Our expedition reaches the mountain from its western side. From Kathmandu you drive to Besisahar, 760 m, in the Marsyangdi river valley, and from there continue over three days to Dharapani, Gowa and Bimtang, 3,590 m, where you stay for a full acclimatization day. On day 8 you cross the Larke La pass, at more than 5,100 m, and descend to Samdo, 3,860 m, in the upper part of the Budhi Gandaki river valley. The next day you continue to Sama Gaun, 3,530 m, the large village at the foot of the mountain, and on day 10 you climb to base camp, 4,800 m.

The approach trek has a double role. It brings the expedition to the mountain, and it is also the first stage of acclimatization: the body climbs gradually, rests a full day in Bimtang, and meets an altitude of more than 5,100 m on the pass before it even reaches base camp. Along the trek you sleep in teahouses, in twin rooms, and the porters carry your personal gear, up to 15 kg per person. In the villages of the upper valley, such as Samdo and Sama Gaun, the culture is Tibetan in character: stone houses, monasteries, mani walls and prayer flags.

The Budhi Gandaki valley is prone to floods and landslides, mainly in the monsoon season and the weeks after it, and they can damage the bridges, trails and roads that lead into the area. Our expedition departs in September, close to the end of the monsoon, so we will say it plainly: the condition of the trails and roads is checked before departure, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides on the ground. We have written separately about the floods in Nepal and what they mean for the trekking season.

content.value: On our route you do not walk the lower part of the valley: you enter it from above, over the pass, and at the end of the expedition you fly by shared helicopter from Sama Gaun to Kathmandu. Anyone who wants to know the full circuit around the mountain, which also runs through the lower part of the valley, will find all the details in our Manaslu Circuit trek guide.

content.value: Base camp, rotations and acclimatization

Manaslu Base Camp lies above Sama Gaun, at 4,800 m. You arrive on day 10 and leave on day 27, so it is home to the expedition for most of the climb. At base camp and at the high camps you sleep in twin tents, and three meals a day, chosen from a menu, are included throughout the climb. Base camp has walkie-talkies and a satellite phone, and the group carries a Magnus satellite device and a pulse oximeter.

The heart of the expedition is days 11 to 23, which are dedicated to rotations. A rotation is a climb to a high camp, a night there and a descent back to base camp to rest. That way the body meets a new altitude, adapts to it and recovers lower down, and each rotation goes higher than the one before. After the rotations you rest at base camp and wait for a good weather window for the summit push. The order of the rotations may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides on the ground.

content.title: ✦ Time for the mountain
content.value: In our itinerary 13 days, days 11 to 23, are dedicated to rotations and acclimatization, and day 26 is kept for bad weather. That time allows the body to acclimatize, and the expedition to wait for a good summit window without giving up the attempt in advance.

The main risk on Manaslu is the altitude itself. Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. At this altitude it can develop into high altitude pulmonary or cerebral edema, so when symptoms get worse, you descend. Our rule is simple: safety before the summit. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching the summit, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.
The camps and the technical sections

The normal route usually has four camps above base camp. Their position changes slightly from season to season, depending on the state of the glacier and the snow: Camp 1 at about 5,500 to 5,700 m, Camp 2 at about 6,250 to 6,400 m, Camp 3 at about 6,800 m, and Camp 4, the high camp, at about 7,450 to 7,500 m.
From base camp to Camp 1

The way climbs over the moraine, the field of rocks the glacier has left behind, and continues on the glacier itself, among crevasses and small ice steps. Above Camp 1 you move almost all the way along fixed ropes.
From Camp 1 to Camp 2: the most technical section

This is the hardest section of the route technically: a steep, broken glacier with ice walls, deep crevasses and hanging blocks of ice. Aluminum ladders are laid over some of the crevasses, and on the steep sections you climb snow and ice slopes with the help of the fixed ropes. The state of the glacier changes from year to year, and with it the number of ladders and the difficulty.

content.caption: A ladder over a crevasse in the glacier, with ropes on both sides

content.value: From Camp 2 to Camp 4

Above Camp 2 the slopes ease, and fixed ropes are set on the steep sections. Camp 3 is usually placed in a spot relatively sheltered from avalanche paths. The section between Camp 3 and Camp 4 is long and steep, and its main danger is avalanches from the northeast face, especially after storms. That is one of the reasons the summit push depends on a window of stable weather.
Climbing gear

On the mountain you climb with full climbing gear: crampons, an ice axe, a harness and a rope ascender, a jumar, which you clip to the fixed ropes, together with high-altitude mountaineering boots and warm down clothing. Personal climbing gear is not included in the price of the expedition, and the fixing of ropes along the route to the summit is included. Anyone coming to Manaslu needs to know this gear well and use it with confidence, even in thick gloves and at the end of a long day.
Oxygen and Sherpa support

On Manaslu expeditions it is common to use bottled oxygen on the upper part of the mountain. Climbers usually start breathing oxygen at the high camp, for the night before summit day, and continue on summit day itself, and some expeditions start as early as Camp 3. With us every climber receives three oxygen bottles, including a mask. Oxygen does not cancel the effect of altitude, but it eases breathing and effort during the long hours of summit day.

Sherpa teams are a central part of every Manaslu expedition, and among other things they fix the ropes along the route. On our expedition every climber has a personal Sherpa guide, on a 1:1 ratio, who accompanies them to the summit. Alongside them work professional local English-speaking guides.

Two payments to the team are not included in the price, and it is worth planning for them in advance: a summit bonus for the guides, 1,500 dollars per person, and tips for guides and porters, 350 dollars per person.

content.caption: Climbers in oxygen masks at sunrise, above the clouds

content.value: Good to know: the expedition is led by professional local English-speaking guides, and a personal Sherpa guide climbs alongside every climber. You need enough English to follow instructions and communicate with the team on the mountain. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory throughout the expedition.
Summit day

When a good weather window opens, you climb from base camp through the camps to the high camp, and set out from there for the summit during the night. From Camp 4 you climb more than 600 vertical meters, at first on relatively gentle slopes, and finally along a narrow, exposed ridge that leads to the summit. This is the most exposed section of the route, and here it is especially important to move slowly, close to the rope and to your Sherpa.

content.alt: A line of headlamps lighting a snow slope in the dark, with a climber in a red suit and a backpack in the foreground
content.caption: A line of headlamps on a snow slope, on a night ascent

content.value: The summit is only halfway. In our itinerary you descend on summit day itself as far as Camp 2, and the next day continue to base camp. Day 26 is a spare day for bad weather, or a rest day at base camp. On day 27 you descend to Sama Gaun, and on day 28 you fly by helicopter to Kathmandu.
Who the expedition suits

Manaslu is not a first mountain. The expedition is meant only for experienced mountaineers who have already gained experience on peaks of 6,000 and 7,000 m, and we grade it as extreme. That experience teaches you how your body reacts to high altitude, to cold and to long days, and builds the habits the mountain demands: walking in crampons, working with a harness and jumar on fixed ropes, and keeping a steady pace for hours.

Beyond experience, the mountain demands excellent fitness, mental preparation and the ability to endure weeks in camps, in the cold and waiting for the weather. A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join. Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call.

If that experience is still ahead of you, you can gain it with us too: in Nepal we run expeditions to peaks above 6,000 m, such as Mera Peak and Island Peak, and to Himlung Himal, a peak above 7,000 m, and in Kyrgyzstan to Lenin Peak, which is also above 7,000 m. We have written a complete guide to Himlung, a good first peak above 7,000 m.

content.value: Permits, visa and insurance

To climb Manaslu you need a climbing permit from the Department of Tourism of Nepal, issued through a registered agency. The price of the permit is set by climbing season and is revised from time to time, and the Manaslu climbing permit, together with the entry permits for the conservation areas the route passes through, is included in the price of our expedition.

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, get a Nepal tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. The expedition spends 30 days in Nepal, every day of a 30-day visa, with no margin for weather days on the mountain, so you need a 90-day visa, which costs 125 US dollars (as of 2026) and is not included. Travel and medical insurance is not included either. Before buying a policy, make sure it covers mountaineering up to 8,163 m, including helicopter rescue and evacuation, and check your government's current travel advice for Nepal before you go.
When to go

Nepal has two main climbing seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. On Manaslu the fall is the main season, and in spring more snow usually falls on the mountain. Our expedition departs in September, so the climbing days themselves fall in the fall season. You will find the current dates on the expedition page.
What it costs and what is included

The Manaslu expedition costs 15,000 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Kathmandu and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, 4 nights in a 4-star hotel in Kathmandu in a single room with breakfast, a shared helicopter flight from Sama Gaun at the end of the expedition, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms throughout the trek, double tents during the climb, dinners at a restaurant before and after the climb, three full meals a day throughout the climb, 2 liters of hot water a day, professional local English-speaking guides, a personal Sherpa guide all the way to the summit, porters for personal gear up to 15 kg per person, showers and toilets in the teahouses where available on the route, all entry permits for the trek and the climb, three oxygen bottles per climber including a mask, fixed ropes along the route to the summit, a first aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, a pulse oximeter for the group, a Magnus satellite device for the group, walkie-talkies and a satellite phone at base camp, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the climb, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear (clothing, footwear, climbing gear and summit boots), tips for guides and porters (350 dollars per person), a summit bonus for the guides (1,500 dollars per person), a 90-day Nepal visa (125 dollars), an extra hotel night if needed, vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet.
In the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.
Manaslu with HighAir

Our Manaslu expedition lasts 30 days, departs in September and is limited to 10 climbers. The success rate we publish on the mountain is 60 to 70 percent, and that is a number worth understanding: the weather, the snow conditions and the condition of each climber decide what happens on the mountain, and safety comes before the summit.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Everyone who has stood on a summit above 8,000 m got there step by step, and mountain by mountain. If the mountains of 6,000 and 7,000 m are already behind you, and Manaslu is the next one, we are here.

content.value: Frequently asked questions
How many days does a Manaslu expedition take?

The HighAir expedition lasts 30 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. It includes an approach trek of about a week over the Larke La pass, 13 days of rotations and acclimatization between the high camps, a summit day, a spare day for bad weather and a helicopter flight from Sama Gaun to Kathmandu at the end.
What experience do you need to climb Manaslu?

The expedition is meant only for experienced climbers who have already gained experience on peaks of 6,000 and 7,000 m. The climb crosses glaciers and crevasses and follows fixed ropes, so you need to know crampons, a harness and a jumar well. Excellent fitness and mental preparation are also required, and a medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure.
Is oxygen used on Manaslu?

Yes. On our expedition every climber receives three oxygen bottles, including a mask, and has a personal Sherpa guide on a 1:1 ratio who accompanies them to the summit. Climbers usually start breathing oxygen at the high camp, ahead of summit day.
When is the season for climbing Manaslu?
The main season on Manaslu is the fall, after the monsoon. There are expeditions in spring too, but more snow usually falls on the mountain then. Our expedition departs in September.
How much does a Manaslu expedition cost?

The price is 15,000 US dollars per person. It includes, among other things, a personal Sherpa guide, three oxygen bottles, fixed ropes, accommodation in teahouses and tents, three meals a day, the climbing permit and a helicopter flight at the end. International flights, insurance, personal gear, the visa, tips and the summit bonus for the guides are not included.
What language do the guides speak?
The expedition is led by professional local English-speaking guides, and a personal Sherpa guide climbs alongside every climber.
